timeline.shipped: Company and competitor research; three prototype concepts
MCP server spec with OAuth design and junk-draft guardrails
Dropped MCP for a no-setup browser demo (reviewers won't connect an AI tool). Dropped the AI-review idea after finding Submittable already ships Smart Reviewer. Wrote this spec.

Repo initialized and pushed to GitHub (github.com/pauljmillar/program-builder). Next.js App Router + TypeScript + Tailwind scaffold. Design tokens and free font substitutes (EB Garamond, Inter, JetBrains Mono) wired in. Page shells for /, /why, /build-log, /how-it-works. CI workflow (lint, typecheck, build), green on main. First production deploy to Vercel (program-builder-gamma.vercel.app), connected to the GitHub repo for auto-deploy on push.

Zod schema for the full program (lib/schema.ts) with JSON Schema export via zod's native toJSONSchema. estimateMinutes formula. All 10 checker rules from spec §6 (lib/validate/rules/*), each with a passing and a breaking Vitest case. Added pnpm test to CI.

Sequential 7-step generation pipeline (lib/generate), one Claude tool-use call per section, versioned prompts (lib/prompts/v1), and the checker + repair loop (max 2 rounds). `pnpm build-program "<prompt>"` runs it end to end. Verified with two real API calls: a clean sample prompt (zero issues on the first pass) and a deliberately contradictory one ("$10,000 fund... awards up to $50,000") that correctly left an unresolvable PROMPT_CONFLICT in `remaining` after 2 repair rounds, rather than silently picking a number.

pnpm record generates the 3 real samples in content/samples/*.json (actual API calls, no fabricated output). Replay UI: StepList, SectionCard, CheckCard, ProgramTabs (Program/JSON/In Submittable), and per-section renderers, orchestrated by ProgramDemo, which replays each sample using its real recorded per-step timings. All 3 samples passed every checker rule on the first try (see finding above) rather than needing a repair-round catch.

50-case eval set (eval/cases.jsonl) matching the spec's category breakdown exactly. pnpm eval runs the full pipeline with bounded concurrency and writes a committed results file. Real v1 baseline: 94% final pass rate, 33% of contradictions caught, $0.098/program. Found and fixed a real bug (the retry fix above), which moved v1 to 94% final pass / 100% schema-valid / 50% contradictions caught. Built and ran prompt v2 as a real comparison — it regressed contradiction-catching to 17%, so v1 stays the default (see finding above). /how-it-works now reads every number from the latest committed eval file, with a real version-comparison chart and 3 real example cases. Added an eval-gate CI workflow that re-runs a fixed 10-case subset for real whenever lib/prompts/** changes, and fails if the pass rate drops more than 10 points against the last committed full run. Copied the MCP server design into docs/mcp-design.md. Caught and fixed a methodology bug in the gate's own pass-rate comparison on its first real CI run (see finding above).

Added the optional "My first 90 days" home-page section (hidden until content/plan.mdx has real content, per spec). Filled in real cost figures in the build log from the 150 real eval cases and 3 recorded samples run so far ($15.35 + $0.29 measured, ideation and the unmeasured ad-hoc debugging calls left as labeled estimates). README updated to match what's actually built (eval:gate, no Playwright claim since no e2e tests exist yet).

Real `lighthouse` runs against the deployed site found and fixed 3 color-contrast failures in the scraped Submittable brand tokens (see finding above) — all 4 pages now score performance 100 / accessibility 100, with LCP 0.4-0.9s. Wired framer-motion's MotionConfig(reducedMotion="user") so animations actually respect the OS setting, not just a CSS override that framer-motion's JS-driven animations would have ignored. Added Vercel Web Analytics plus sample_clicked and lets_talk_clicked custom events. Replaced the fake "Watch 45 seconds" link (which just scrolled to the samples) with an honest modal admitting the video isn't recorded yet.

tools.usedFor: Scaffold, schema, checker, generation pipeline, UI, eval harness, deployment

failures.title: CI failed on first push: conflicting pnpm versions
failures.whatHappened: The CI workflow pinned `pnpm/action-setup@v4` to version 10 while package.json's `packageManager` field pinned pnpm@10.32.1. pnpm's own version check treats those as two different sources of truth and refuses to run.
failures.howCaught: First GitHub Actions run on main failed immediately in the 'Run pnpm/action-setup@v4' step, before lint/typecheck/build even started.
failures.fix: Dropped the explicit `version: 10` from the workflow step so action-setup reads the version from package.json's packageManager field instead.
failures.lesson: When package.json already pins a packageManager version, don't also pin it in CI config — pick one source of truth.

failures.title: CI typecheck failed: Next.js's generated route types weren't there yet
failures.whatHappened: `app/layout.tsx` uses Next.js's typed-routes `LayoutProps<'/'>` global, which only exists once Next.js has generated `.next/types` (gitignored). CI ran a standalone `tsc --noEmit` before anything had generated those types, so it failed on `Cannot find name 'LayoutProps'` even though `pnpm build` passed fine locally (build generates the types itself first).
failures.howCaught: Second CI run still failed, now in the typecheck step specifically, right after fixing the pnpm version issue.
failures.fix: Added a `next typegen` step before `pnpm typecheck` in CI, which generates just the route types without a full build.
failures.lesson: A typed-routes feature means `tsc --noEmit` alone isn't a complete typecheck in CI — it depends on a generation step that `next build`/`next dev` normally does implicitly.

failures.title: PROMPT_CONFLICT checker misread its own award-amount match as the fund total
failures.whatHappened: The PROMPT_CONFLICT rule's regex extraction scans every "$X" mention for nearby words like "fund" or "total" to guess the stated funding total. It didn't exclude mentions already claimed by the award-amount regexes ("up to $X", a "$X-$Y" range), so a prompt like "A fund for nonprofits. Awards up to $25,000" misread the award figure as the fund total too, because the word "fund" fell inside that mention's context window.
failures.howCaught: Unit test for PROMPT_CONFLICT (tests/unit/promptConflict.test.ts): a case asserting the award-max mismatch message contained both the expected and actual numbers failed because the extractor also fired a false fundingTotal mismatch, producing the wrong message at index 0.
failures.fix: Tracked the index ranges already claimed by award-amount matches and skip any money mention inside those ranges when scanning for a fund total.
failures.lesson: A regex-based extractor needs to track which spans of text it's already consumed, or a second heuristic pass will double-count the same number under a different label.

failures.title: First live API calls rejected the tool schema and the forced tool_choice
failures.whatHappened: Three real 400s from the Anthropic API on the first live run of the generation pipeline: (1) zod's exclusiveMinimum keyword (from `.positive()`) isn't supported in a tool's input_schema; (2) setting `strict: true` on the tool turned on a much more restricted schema subset that rejected even plain `minimum`; (3) with strict mode removed, the forced `tool_choice: {type: "tool", name}` itself came back "not supported for this model."
failures.howCaught: Running `pnpm build-program` against a real sample prompt with a real API key, per spec §0.7 — not caught by any unit test, since those don't hit the live API.
failures.fix: Changed `.positive()` to `.min(1)` in lib/schema.ts, dropped `strict: true` from the tool definition, and dropped the forced tool_choice entirely (tool_choice defaults to "auto", and with exactly one tool offered the model calls it every time in practice).
failures.lesson: The SDK's types don't tell you which JSON Schema keywords or tool_choice modes a given model actually accepts — that only shows up by calling the real API. Budget for this on any new model or SDK version.

failures.title: pnpm record failed on a real sample: the model sent a number as a quoted string
failures.whatHappened: The first real `pnpm record` run failed with a ZodError: `expectedApplications` came back from the model as the string "100" instead of the number 100, which `z.number()` correctly rejects. Nothing in the tool's JSON Schema forbids a numeric string, and the model treated it as an acceptable way to write the number.
failures.howCaught: Running the actual sample-recording script against the live API, not a unit test — the test fixtures only ever construct well-typed objects directly.
failures.fix: Switched every model-drafted numeric field in lib/schema.ts from `z.number()` to `z.coerce.number()` (fundingTotal, awardMin, awardMax, expectedApplications, maxWords, weight, order, reviewersPerApplication, panelSize, estimatedMinutes). Confirmed the JSON Schema output is unchanged (still `type: "number"`) and that it still correctly rejects non-numeric strings.
failures.lesson: A model filling in a JSON Schema's `type: "number"` can still hand back a numeric-looking string. Coerce at the validation boundary rather than trusting the type the schema asked for.

failures.title: The 3 canonical samples pass every check on the first try — no fabricated "catch" added
failures.whatHappened: The spec's demo mock-up shows the climate fund sample catching and fixing a rubric problem. In practice, across multiple real recordings (including a manual retry), all 3 canonical sample prompts (climate fund, Kestrel County, Northwind scholarship) generate clean on the first pass: zero errors, zero warnings, nothing for the repair loop to do.
failures.howCaught: `pnpm record` and a manual rerun of the climate-fund prompt, both against the live API.
failures.fix: Did not invent or inject an issue to force a "catch" moment, per spec §0.3 (never fabricate results). Left the Check card able to show a clean pass as a good outcome ("Passed every check on the first pass"). The real catch-and-repair demonstration lives in the eval set's deliberately-contradictory cases instead — verified directly with a test prompt ("$10,000 fund... awards up to $50,000"), where the checker correctly left an unresolved PROMPT_CONFLICT after 2 repair rounds rather than silently picking a number.
failures.lesson: A strong model with well-scoped prompts will often just get well-posed inputs right the first time — the checker's value shows up on messier or contradictory input, not on hand-picked clean demo prompts. Don't force a canned failure into a demo that doesn't naturally have one.

failures.title: First full 50-case eval: 3 cases failed because the model didn't call the tool at all
failures.whatHappened: The first real `pnpm eval v1` run (schema-valid rate 94%, final pass rate 90%) had 3 outright failures, all the same root cause: the model responded with plain text instead of a tool_use block. Two were extremely terse one-line prompts ("Help small businesses recover.", "Support for first-generation college students.") where the model apparently preferred to ask a clarifying question. The third was a repair call on a genuinely impossible award range ($60,000 max from a $40,000 fund), where the model seems to have balked at "fixing" something unfixable rather than picking a resolution.
failures.howCaught: `pnpm eval` against the real 50-case set, not any unit test — this needed real model variance across real prompts to surface.
failures.fix: Added a one-time retry in lib/generate/callStructured.ts: if a call comes back with no tool_use block, retry once with an explicit nudge not to decline and to make a reasonable assumption. Re-ran the full eval afterward: schema-valid rate went 94% -> 100%, final pass rate 90% -> 94%, contradictions caught 33% -> 50% (both committed results files are kept, so this improvement is visible in the eval history, not just asserted).
failures.lesson: Even with exactly one tool offered, a model can still choose not to call it, especially on vague or genuinely contradictory input. A retry-with-a-nudge is cheap insurance; the real fix for vagueness is a clearer instruction to always produce an answer, which also shaped prompt v2.

failures.title: Prompt v2 made the eval numbers worse, not better — kept v1 as the default
failures.whatHappened: v2 added one instruction to every prompt: always call the tool and make a reasonable, defensible assumption, even on genuinely contradictory or vague input (the fix for the vague-prompt failures above). On the full 50-case eval, v2's schema-valid rate and final pass rate both came in slightly below v1, and contradictions caught dropped from 50% to 17%. The same instruction that stopped the model from refusing also made it more willing to quietly resolve a stated contradiction during generation — e.g. picking consistent numbers instead of reproducing the prompt's contradictory ones — which means the checker has nothing left to catch. That's the opposite of what this product needs: contradictions should surface for a human, not get smoothed over.
failures.howCaught: Running the full v2 eval and comparing it to the v1 baseline, both committed for real (content/eval/results-v1-2026-11-02.json vs results-v2-2026-11-02.json).
failures.fix: Kept v1 as the default prompt version (lib/generate/pipeline.ts's PROMPT_VERSION). v2 stays committed as a real, uncherry-picked comparison point — the retry fix in callStructured.ts (a code change, not a prompt change) is what actually fixed the vague-prompt failures, and it applies to both versions equally.
failures.lesson: An instruction that fixes one failure mode (refusing to answer) can quietly create another (resolving contradictions it should be surfacing). Measuring the full eval before adopting a prompt change caught this; adopting v2 on the strength of the vague-prompt fix alone would have shipped a regression.

failures.title: eval-gate's first real CI run failed on a methodology bug, not a real regression
failures.whatHappened: The eval-gate workflow's first live run (triggered by the lib/prompts/v2 commit) failed: 80% subset pass rate vs. a 94% full-run baseline, an apparent 14-point drop. But 2 of the 10 subset cases are deliberately-contradictory prompts (a $10K fund with a $50K award cap; awardMin > awardMax) where "finalPassed: false" is the correct outcome — the checker is supposed to leave those unresolved for a human, not quietly fix them. The gate compared raw finalPassed rates, so a subset with a heavier mix of contradictory cases than the full 50-case set looked worse for a reason that had nothing to do with quality.
failures.howCaught: The eval-gate GitHub Actions run itself failing on the very commit that added prompt v2 — the first time this gate ran for real.
failures.fix: Added `caseSucceeded()` in eval/types.ts: for a case with mustFlag entries, success means every expected code was caught (regardless of finalPassed); for an ordinary case, success still means finalPassed. Rewrote both the subset run and the baseline comparison in eval/gate.ts to use this instead of raw finalPassed rates.
failures.lesson: A quality gate that mixes an unconditionally-good outcome (passing cleanly) with a conditionally-good one (correctly flagging something unfixable) needs to know which one applies to a given case, or a subset with a different case mix than the baseline will produce false alarms.

failures.title: Submittable's own scraped brand colors fail WCAG AA contrast as text
failures.whatHappened: Running a real Lighthouse audit (not a guess — `npx lighthouse` against the deployed site with Chrome) found 3 real color-contrast failures, all from using Submittable's actual scraped hex values as text: --blue-gray (#8a92a2) as secondary/body text only hits ~3:1 on our light backgrounds and ~3:1 again in the one place it sits on a dark background (the footer) for the opposite reason; --signal-blue (#2e73eb) as link text hits ~4.0-4.4:1; the coral primary button (#fc5b30 bg, white text) hits ~3.1:1. All need 4.5:1 for normal-size text.
failures.howCaught: A real `lighthouse` run against the deployed production URL, scoring 95/100 accessibility with color-contrast as the only failing audit — then confirmed the specific failing elements from the audit's own detail output.
failures.fix: Darkened --blue-gray to #55606e and --signal-blue to #2257b8 in app/globals.css (both are only ever used as text or as non-text UI needing the lower 3:1 threshold, so darkening doesn't break their other uses). Switched the footer's one dark-background label to --cadet-grey, which already had enough contrast against deep-blue. Bumped the two coral CTA buttons to 19px bold, which crosses WCAG's large-text threshold and drops the requirement to 3:1 — already cleared without changing the brand color at all. Re-ran Lighthouse after each fix until color-contrast actually passed on all 4 pages, not just assumed fixed.
failures.lesson: A brand's real production colors aren't guaranteed to pass accessibility as text — verify with an actual contrast calculation (or a real audit tool) rather than assuming a scraped hex value is safe to reuse as-is for text, even when it's accurately copied from the source.
